candidates.title: PRT bridge fetches, keeps and rescans every log of the shared, permissionless tournament factory on every observation, so the honest player's cost grows with chain activity that does not belong to the application
candidates.component: PRT bridge (doc/recipes/prt-bridge.lua methods:observe, with prt-log-history.lua), started by prt-epoch.lua / crisium.lua
candidates.role: Support (AUDIT.md: 'The PRT player and bridge in doc/recipes ... Support'). Section 3: a support defect is Medium 'when it would rate High or Critical in the role the component stands in for, such as ... the honest operator for an implementation of an operator'. The bridge stands in for the honest operator's chain observation.
candidates.location: doc/recipes/prt-bridge.lua methods:observe (line 57: addresses = { self.factory, self.consensus, self.root }, first_blocks[self.factory] = self.first_block; lines 69-102 loop over every fetched log; line 110 table.sort(logs, log_less) over all of them; the decoded TournamentCreated events of foreign tournaments are added to snapshot.events and walked again by methods:jobs and report_lost_matches). prt-epoch.lua:126 sets first_block = seal_block, so the factory is fetched from the seal to the head for the whole life of the dispute. prt-log-history.lua keeps every fetched log in self.logs[address] until a reset, and a reset (any removed log, any non-canonical head) refetches all of them. The factory address comes from consensus.getTournamentFactory (crisium.lua:124). Dave: MultiLevelTournamentFactory.instantiate (prt/contracts/src/tournament/factories/MultiLevelTournamentFactory.sol:79-92) is external with no access control and emits TournamentCreated; cartesi-rollups/contracts/script/Deployment.s.sol deploys one factory (create2) that DaveAppFactory uses for every Dave application, so every application's epoch seal also logs there.
candidates.description: The bridge needs exactly one factory log, the TournamentCreated of its own root tournament (it ignores every other TournamentCreated: `if name == "NewInnerTournament" or address == self.root`). TournamentCreated has no indexed field, so the request cannot filter it, yet the bridge keeps the factory in the address set of every observation after the root's creation was observed. Every TournamentCreated that any party causes on the shared factory between the seal and the end of the dispute is fetched, stored in the history for the life of the bridge, decoded once (0.13 ms each with the real ABI), copied into the snapshot's logs and events and sorted on EVERY observation. Observations run at least once per block and several times per job (tick -> refresh loop -> attempt -> refresh). The per-observation cost and the bridge's memory are therefore linear in the number of foreign factory logs since the seal, and the total over a dispute is quadratic in it. Nothing in the bridge depends on those logs.
candidates.trigger: Any party (an adversary, or simply the other applications deployed through the same DaveAppFactory) calls MultiLevelTournamentFactory.instantiate during an open dispute of the application. Each call is a cloneWithImmutableArgs deployment (on the order of 1e5-2e5 gas, an estimate, not measured), cheap on an L2. The adversary capability 'Raise activity on the chain that does not belong to the application, such as inputs to other applications that share its input record' (section 7) covers it.
candidates.reachability: Reachable from the genesis of any deployment: instantiate is permissionless and the factory is the one the consensus names. No state of the machine is involved.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? No exclusion applies. The trigger is chain activity by other parties, which section 7 grants the adversary ('Raise activity on the chain that does not belong to the application'); it does not need an untrusted caller of the machine API, a snapshot, a reorg or a host fault. The node only relays the logs (section 4: 'data relayed by the node from others' is untrusted).

2 Role: the PRT bridge is Support per AUDIT.md; it stands in for the honest operator's chain observation, so it is rated at most Medium ('A defect that only a support component shows is never above Medium').

3 High/Medium cases: as a support defect, section 3 makes it Medium if it would be High or Critical for the honest operator. For the honest operator it is not one of the High cases: it is not a constant-factor increase of an R12 emulator operation but the 'honest operator's own work outside the emulator', whose growth R12 forbids outright.

4 Critical (in the stood-in role): R12 'The honest operator's own work outside the emulator, such as observing the chain, keeping and persisting its own records, and restarting, has a bounded cost per input, per yield, and per match, and its total grows only with the inputs, yields, and matches of the epochs still open. That total must not grow with the application's age, with the number of past epochs, or with chain activity that does not belong to the application.' The bridge's per-observation time and memory grow linearly with foreign TournamentCreated logs and without bound in an adversary's spend. On the honest operator's path ('Observing the chain'), a slowdown that makes the player miss its clocks is a completeness failure (section 1: 'cannot respond in time'). Critical for the honest operator, therefore Medium for this support component.
5 Low: not applicable (step 4 applied). If triage holds that a demo bridge's observation cost has no R12 bearing, it is Low.
candidates.threat_to_goal: If a production validator copied this observation design, an adversary who spams the shared factory (or merely a busy multi-application chain) would make every observation of every open dispute slower and heavier, up to missing the response windows (completeness failure: the honest claim loses by timeout and a dishonest claim can win). In the recipe it violates R12's explicit ban on cost growing with unrelated chain activity.
candidates.evidence: Ran bridge.new_observer(...):observe() (the code the honest bridge uses) on a mock chain whose factory holds the root's TournamentCreated plus N foreign TournamentCreated logs after it (script exp/factory-spam.lua in the scratch directory). N=1000: repeated observe 6.5 ms, 1002 logs/events in the snapshot, 2 MB; N=10000: 78 ms, 15 MB; N=100000: 1.07 s per observation, 137 MB, every foreign log in snapshot.logs and snapshot.events. Decoding (cached per log) of a real TournamentCreated with the released Dave ABI costs 0.126 ms (exp/decode-cost.lua), so a first observation or any post-reset observation of 100000 logs adds about 13 s.
candidates.test_idea: bugs/<ID>/test.lua: build a bridge with bridge.new_observer over a mock chain (as prt-bridge-test.lua's pruning fixture does) whose factory emits the root's TournamentCreated, then N=10000 TournamentCreated logs of other tournaments in later blocks. Count the factory logs the chain hands out on a second observation after the root was observed, and the length of snapshot.logs/events. Required (R12): neither depends on N (e.g. assert #snapshot.logs < 100 and no factory request after the root's creation is final). Exit 1 on audit/prt2 (they equal N+2).

candidates.title: PRT player keeps one hash per output of the current input in memory, so a guest can make the claim computation's memory grow with the number of outputs
candidates.component: PRT player (doc/recipes/prt.lua, run_to_input_mcycle_offset / run_next_input, used by the stored honest player of crisium.lua and by the forked player)
candidates.role: Support (AUDIT.md: 'The PRT player ... Support'); stands in for the honest operator, which computes the claim on this path.
candidates.location: doc/recipes/prt.lua run_to_input_mcycle_offset (line 2066 onward): `pending_output_hashes[#pending_output_hashes + 1] = keccak(output_data)` at line 2088 for every automatic yield with reason tx-output, kept until the input's fixed point, then flush_pending_outputs (line 1419) pushes them into the outputs frontier. run_next_input (line 2243) passes last_output and self.outputs_frontier, so the table is built on the epoch run that computes the mcycle claim. Each automatic yield also copies up to the declared length (at most the tx buffer, 2 MiB) through receive_cmio_request into a Lua string before the reason is checked (run_to_stop, line 1396).
candidates.description: The outputs of an input are appended, as 32-byte Lua strings, to an unbounded Lua array until the input yields manually, because they must be discarded if the input is rejected. The array grows by roughly 70 bytes per output (string object plus array slot) with no cap. An input whose guest emits outputs in a tight loop (each output is a few instructions and one automatic yield) makes the honest player's resident memory linear in the number of outputs of that single input: 1e8 outputs, about 1e9 mcycles, need about 7 GB; the outputs frontier itself is O(log). An out-of-memory kill of the player during the epoch run repeats on every relaunch at the same input, so the player never seals the epoch and never posts or defends its claim. A frontier copy (O(63) hashes) taken at the input boundary would give the same discard-on-reject semantics in constant memory.
candidates.trigger: An input sender whose input takes control of the guest (section 4: 'Any input may take control of the firmware, the kernel, the rollup libraries, and the application'), or an application that emits many outputs, emits a large number of tx-output automatic yields within one input.
candidates.reachability: Any assignment of guest-writable memory and registers is presumed reachable; the guest executes an automatic yield with reason tx-output in a loop. The yield is a documented device command. The mcycles needed (about 10 per output) stay far below the per-input limit (2^48) and within the per-input usage that real Linux applications are sized for (1e9-1e10).
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? The exclusion 'An application that tries to exhaust the honest operator through the number of its outputs or yields ... This holds as long as the memory and storage that the honest operator needs to defend its claims do not grow with the number of outputs, and each yield costs it a bounded amount (R12)' does not apply, because its own condition fails: the memory grows with the number of outputs. The exclusion of applications that are not correctly designed covers 'only what such an application gets', 'never an emulator defect that its guest triggers', and the honest operator 'still defends the trajectory ... for any application'.
2 Role: the PRT player is Support per AUDIT.md, standing in for the honest operator (it computes claims), so at most Medium.

3 High/Medium cases: Medium for a support component when the defect would be High or Critical in the honest-operator role. It is not one of the High cases there: not a constant-factor increase of an R12 emulator operation but a memory growth that R12 forbids.

4 Critical (in the stood-in role): R12 'The memory and storage the honest operator needs to defend its claims do not grow with the number of outputs.' R4 'This holds for every guest, whether or not its application is correctly designed'. An OOM during the epoch run stops the claim computation, a completeness failure (section 1). Also section 8 Critical list: 'unbounded allocation caused by data from other parties that the honest operator must process' (the input that drives the guest). Critical for the honest operator, therefore Medium here.

5 Low: not applicable. If triage reads the output exclusion as covering any output-driven cost of a support player, it would be Low; the deciding fact is that the exclusion is conditioned on memory not growing with outputs.
candidates.threat_to_goal: A single input that makes the guest emit very many outputs exhausts the player's memory while it computes the epoch's claim; the relaunched player hits the same input and fails again, so the honest claim is never posted or defended and a dishonest claim can win. It directly violates R12's output clause.
candidates.evidence: Code reading only (no run). The array has no bound; run_next_input -> run_to_input_mcycle_offset passes last_output, which installs on_yield_automatic that appends keccak(output_data) per tx-output yield.
candidates.test_idea: Build a bare-metal guest (bugs/harness/baremetal/build.sh) that, on each advance input, emits K zero-length outputs (cm_yield_automatic with the tx-output reason) and then accepts with any root. Create a forked or in-memory player over it (prt.new_forked_player with a dapp contract whose template is that guest), deliver one input through event_handler.input_added and run it, sampling collectgarbage('count') inside the yield callback (or wrapping keccak to record #pending_output_hashes through a debug hook). Required: peak Lua memory during the input is independent of K (assert growth < 1 MiB between K=1e4 and K=1e6). Exit 1 on audit/prt2 (growth about 70 bytes x K).

candidates.title: crisium keeps and rescans every consensus log since the deployment block, so the player's observation memory and work grow with the application's age
candidates.role: Support (AUDIT.md: the PRT player and bridge are Support); stands in for the honest operator's chain observation.
candidates.location: doc/recipes/crisium.lua lines 207-219: seal_history = log_history.new(chain); get_seal(number) calls seal_history:get_logs(consensus, first_block) with first_block = consensus.getDeploymentBlockNumber() (line 125) and decodes (abi:event, uncached here) every consensus log since deployment on each call; prt-log-history.lua never prunes self.logs. open_epochs calls get_seal once for each newly opened epoch, and a relaunch refetches everything from the deployment block.
candidates.description: The history of the consensus is kept from the deployment block for the life of the process and rescanned (and re-decoded) once per new epoch. The consensus emits EpochSealed and EpochStaged every epoch and SentryClaim per sentry per epoch, so memory is O(past epochs), each epoch costs O(past epochs) of decoding and a relaunch costs O(past epochs) of log requests. Only the seal of the previous epoch is needed.
candidates.trigger: Time: every sealed epoch of the application, plus sentry claims. Not amplifiable by an arbitrary party (submitSentryClaim is restricted to sentries).
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? No exclusion applies (no API misuse, no snapshot, no reorg, no host fault).
2 Role: Support per AUDIT.md, standing in for the honest operator; at most Medium.
3 High/Medium cases: Medium for a support component if Critical or High for the honest operator; none of the listed High cases fits.

4 Critical (in the stood-in role): R12 '[the honest operator's own work outside the emulator] must not grow with the application's age, with the number of past epochs'. The growth is literal but small per epoch (a few logs), so the practical threat needs a very old application or many sentries.

5 Low: if triage weighs the magnitude (a few hundred bytes and a few decodes per past epoch), Low. Both readings: Medium by the letter of R12, Low by impact; the deciding fact is whether R12's growth ban is read as absolute.
candidates.threat_to_goal: Over a long-lived application the player's startup and per-epoch observation costs grow without bound, which R12 forbids because it eventually eats into the clocks A7 sized; a relaunch (part of the honest operator's path, O2) becomes slower with age.
candidates.test_idea: Drive crisium's get_seal logic (or extract it) over a mock chain with E epochs of EpochSealed/EpochStaged logs; count the logs requested and decoded by the call that opens epoch E. Required: independent of E (e.g. it reads from the previous seal's block). Exit 1 on audit/prt2 (it reads all E epochs' logs).

not_covered: JSON-RPC server (cartesi-jsonrpc-machine / jsonrpc-remote-machine.cpp) per-method parsing of every request field: only checked that body size is unlimited by design (trusted caller) and spot-checked exception handling; did not audit every handler for uncaught exceptions or truncations (e.g. data length > 4 GiB cast to uint32 in remote send_cmio_response, not chain-reachable since InputBox caps inputs at 64 KiB).

JSON-RPC client (jsonrpc-machine.cpp) parsing of server replies, including hash_tree_proof parsing that allocates (log2_root_size - log2_target_size) sibling slots up to INT_MAX before checking the array (server is trusted, so not pursued).

Binary step-log verifier (replay-step-state-access.hpp, cm_verify_step): read the header/page/sibling validation and root recomputation, found it bounded; did not audit the interpreter replay paths (TLB, page lookups) under adversarial page contents.
uarch-replay / replay-send-cmio state access: checked access-range, sibling-count and data-size checks; did not fuzz or run ASan on crafted logs.

Lua bindings: checked JSON<->Lua conversion depth limits (256), NUL handling, length checks on send/log/verify_send_cmio_response; did not audit every other clua method for luaL_error longjmp across C++ frames with non-trivial destructors.
prt-websocket.lua and prt-rpc.lua framing (the node is trusted by section 4, so only relayed log contents were considered).

The referee model's transport (game-transport.lua): noticed unbounded line accumulation in receive_line and an assert on abrupt connection loss, which the threat model rates as support stalls of the model (Low); not reported.

cartesi.evmu ABI decoder: dynamic arrays with aliased offsets give quadratic output size, but no event or call the bridge decodes from other parties has a dynamic array, so it is unreachable from adversarial data; not reported.

Fault isolation inside one crisium process: any Lua error in any epoch's listener or bridge (e.g. the assert that native and Solidity transition verification agree in prt-bridge.lua methods:attempt) aborts every epoch and repeats after relaunch; I found no adversary-controlled trigger, so it is not reported, but a native-verifier/Solidity disagreement would turn into an honest crash loop there.

Per-yield cost of the player: every automatic yield copies up to 2 MiB from the tx buffer into Lua (and hashes tx outputs); bounded per yield, so probably covered by the output/yield exclusion; not measured.
machine-guest-tools (libcmt / rollup parsing of rx buffer contents) and the Dave/rollups contracts' own ABI decoding were not audited under this angle.
